comparison: Both strongly support the generation of gene-specific split-GAL4 driver lines (C3, C41, C47, C119-C123). OpenEval focuses on methodological documentation and validation, while peer reviewers emphasize the achievement ('successfully achieved their aims') and the compelling evidence after revision. High agreement on this foundational claim.

Both strongly support the scRNA-seq analysis and hemilineage marker identification (C43-C46, C79-C81, C84, C93-C95, C115-C117). OpenEval emphasizes systematic documentation in figures and tables. Peer reviewers call this work 'gorgeous' and 'astounding,' praising the integration of anatomical knowledge with transcriptional profiles. Complete agreement with high enthusiasm from peers.

Both support the systematic testing and validation of split-GAL4 combinations (C48-C50, C125-C130). OpenEval highlights comprehensive documentation in Table 1 and Figure 3. Peer reviewers affirm developmental stability and specificity as key strengths, with the editor confirming 'compelling' evidence. Strong agreement on temporal stability and specificity.

Both support validation of driver line specificity. OpenEval focuses on 23B driver validation (C55-C75) with immunostaining evidence. Peer reviewers address broader specificity claims (C57, C62, C72, C74, C75) across the toolkit. Overlapping support for specificity validation, though OpenEval is more focused on single example while peers address general property.

Both support the developmental analysis of 4B neurons (C132, C138, C140-C147). OpenEval provides detailed description of morphological progression documented in Figure 4. Peer reviewers accept this as demonstration of toolkit utility for developmental studies without specific critique. Complete agreement on this application.

Both support neurotransmitter mapping using split-GAL4 intersections (C149, C151-C153). OpenEval describes the specific patterns shown in Figure 5. Peer reviewers affirm this as successful demonstration of toolkit utility for assessing neurotransmitter identity. Agreement on this functional application.

Both support general utility claims about the driver lines. OpenEval addresses C5-C6 regarding morphological and neurotransmitter applications. Peer R4 includes C5 in context of developmental analysis. Both treat these as validated applications of the toolkit.

Both support toolkit utility claims. OpenEval R14 addresses C6 about neurotransmitter mapping. Peer R5 addresses C6 and related neurotransmitter claims (C148-C153, C158). Both affirm this as successful demonstration without concerns.

Both support behavioral characterization of 8B neurons (C165, C169, C171-C175). OpenEval notes the jump behavior documentation but flags C175 (participation in GF circuit) as speculative requiring connectome support. Peer reviewers strongly support this work without expressing concern about speculation, treating the behavioral mapping as key demonstration of toolkit value.

Both support systematic behavioral characterization (C7, C52, C166-C168). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive documentation in Table 2 and videos. Peer reviewers affirm behavioral mapping as demonstration of toolkit utility, with particular praise for the 8B-GF connection. Strong agreement on the value of this functional characterization.

Both support the connectome analysis of 8B-GF connectivity (C176-C183). OpenEval notes quantitative documentation but flags C183 (functional interpretation) as inferential. Peer reviewers explicitly praise this integration as 'an excellent example of the utility of this study' without expressing concerns about inferential aspects. Agreement on data quality, peers more enthusiastic about interpretations.

Both support 9A behavioral phenotypes (C185-C187). OpenEval notes consistency with prior studies. Peer reviewers accept these behavioral characterizations as part of comprehensive lineage-behavior mapping demonstrating toolkit utility. Agreement on validation of driver line and confirmation of previous findings.

Both support clonal analysis of 12A neurons (C189-C195). OpenEval notes limited sample size but supports conclusion about multifunctional control. Peer reviewers accept this as supporting evidence for toolkit utility in functional studies without raising sample size concerns. Agreement on findings, peers less critical of limitations.

Both support 21A functional characterization (C197-C204). OpenEval emphasizes convergence of gain-of-function and loss-of-function approaches. Peer reviewers accept these as part of comprehensive behavioral characterization demonstrating toolkit utility. Strong agreement on the quality of this functional validation.

Both support applicability to SEZ (C205-C211). OpenEval notes reasonable inference based on developmental homology. Peer reviewers implicitly support broader applicability through editor's statement about tools being used 'outside the nervous system' and transferability to other fields. Agreement on extensibility, though peers don't specifically address SEZ.

Both support future utility and applications (C8, C39, C217, C219-C220, C223-C224, C236-C242). OpenEval treats these as reasonable speculation grounded in demonstrated properties. Peer reviewers strongly affirm future utility with editor noting transferability to other fields and Reviewer 2 calling it 'a trojan horse to integrate the fields of neural development and systems neuroscience.' Strong agreement with high enthusiasm from peers.

OpenEval supports that scRNA-seq cluster markers correspond to specific hemilineages (C87, C91, C97-C100, C104-C105, C107, C111, C113) with validation in Figure 2. No corresponding peer review result specifically addresses this claim set, though peer R2 discusses related marker identification work more broadly.

OpenEval supports heterogeneity within hemilineages (C108-C114, C234-C235) with differential Tj expression evidence. No corresponding peer review result specifically addresses within-hemilineage heterogeneity, though this relates to the broader validation work praised by peers.

OpenEval supports claims about limitations of existing tools (C2, C13, C31-C38) establishing rationale for the work. No corresponding peer review result specifically addresses these background/motivation claims, though peers implicitly accept the rationale by praising the toolkit's novelty and utility.

OpenEval supports claims about prior foundational work (C40, C53-C54, C76-C78) from authors' previous publications. No corresponding peer review result specifically addresses this background material, though peers acknowledge the authors' 'deep collective knowledge' that enabled the current work.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN the claim that Acj6 is dispensable for neurotransmitter identity (C157) due to data not shown, and notes caveats about Trojan exon method (C159). No corresponding peer review result addresses these specific claims about Acj6 or methodological limitations.
